summary:
ShadeShift is a local urban-cooling experiment in a ~14.7 km² pilot area in Thủ Đức, Ho Chi Minh City. Rather than building another heat map, we asked which satellite signals were stable enough to support a defensible planning shortlist.

We used OlmoEarth annual 10 m embeddings to map reliable built, vegetation, and water cover, tested NASA ECOSTRESS nighttime temperature observations, and validated NASA/USGS Landsat 8/9 daytime Surface Temperature across multiple dates. ECOSTRESS did not show sufficient temporal persistence for our core ranking, so we deliberately downgraded it to contextual evidence. Landsat did survive the repeatability tests and became our thermal core.

After also catching and fixing a boundary-cell ranking artifact, ShadeShift ranks 51 eligible 500 m cells using 60% persistent heat and 40% current greening need, while keeping evidence quality separate from priority. The interactive product lets planners compare signals, inspect 10 m surface evidence, and see caveats rather than hiding uncertainty.
details:
ShadeShift began with a deliberately limited question: before attempting a city-scale urban-heat product, could we take one small and spatially diverse area of Thủ Đức, Ho Chi Minh City, and determine which satellite signals were actually stable enough to help prioritize urban-cooling investigation?

We selected a pilot of roughly 14.7 km² containing dense built surfaces, vegetation, waterways, transport infrastructure, and sharp land-cover transitions. The area is large enough to contain meaningful spatial variation, but small enough that we could audit the evidence cell by cell instead of trusting a citywide model that would be difficult to inspect.

WHAT WE DEVELOPED

ShadeShift is an evidence-aware planning prototype that ranks 500 m cells according to two separate questions:

  1. Does the cell show persistent daytime heat relative to the rest of the pilot?
  2. Does the cell show a current shortage of reliable vegetation relative to built cover?

The frozen priority score is intentionally transparent:

Priority = 60% persistent daytime heat + 40% current greening need.

The score is a relative investigation priority inside this pilot area. It is not a calibrated heat-health risk probability, a prediction of cooling impact, or a recommendation for an exact tree-planting location.

THE EXPERIMENTAL JOURNEY

Our first major component was current land-cover evidence. We used OlmoEarth v1.3 annual 10 m Earth-observation embeddings and trained a simple logistic-regression classifier to distinguish vegetation, built surfaces, and water. Pixels without sufficient support or confidence remain unknown rather than being forced into a class.

Under our weak multi-source consensus labeling protocol, the frozen classifier reached a held-out macro-F1 of approximately 0.958, while 200 group-aware resampling experiments produced a mean macro-F1 of approximately 0.948. These values measure agreement with our weak consensus labels, not independent human ground truth. We deliberately preserve that distinction in the project.

Next, we tested NASA ECOSTRESS Version 2 Land Surface Temperature observations. ECOSTRESS was initially attractive because of its thermal detail, but the relative hotspot patterns in our usable nighttime scenes did not persist reliably between dates at either 70 m or our 500 m planning scale. Instead of selecting a visually convenient scene, we treated that result as a failed hypothesis. ECOSTRESS was therefore downgraded to contextual nighttime evidence and is not used in the core priority score.

We then tested Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Temperature. Core acquisition dates were selected using quality and coverage rules before we measured agreement, avoiding the temptation to choose scenes because they produced a preferred pattern. At 500 m, the selected Landsat dates produced substantially stronger temporal repeatability. The median pairwise Spearman correlation among the five moderate-quality core dates was approximately 0.664, and a stricter guarded-quality subset remained strongly consistent. Landsat therefore became our validated thermal core.

For every validated acquisition, we aggregate the thermal anomaly to 500 m cells, rank cells within the spatially supported pilot area, and take the median percentile rank across dates. This makes the thermal signal a multi-date relative consensus rather than a claim based on one “best” satellite image or precise neighborhood temperature.

THE BUG THAT CHANGED OUR RESULT

An important part of our project was discovering that our first supposedly finished ranking was wrong.

A spatial audit found that several boundary cells overlapped the actual evidence raster by only tiny slivers, yet were still represented as full 500 m planning cells. Some of these cells received extreme heat or land-cover values and entered the Top 10.

Across the original 80 cells, 18 had less than 50% footprint support. Six of the then-current Top 10 were affected boundary cells.

We reopened the pipeline, introduced a minimum 50% footprint-overlap requirement, recomputed thermal percentile ranks only over spatially supported cells, and reran our sensitivity analysis. The final pipeline retained 62 spatially supported cells and 51 fully eligible ranked cells.

This correction became central to ShadeShift's philosophy: a result should not remain in the product simply because it looks useful. It has to survive the evidence checks.

EVIDENCE QUALITY IS NOT THE SAME AS PRIORITY

ShadeShift also assigns a product-facing evidence grade to each eligible cell. The grade considers temporal stability, same-date stricter quality-screen corroboration, and spatial support.

The final 51 eligible cells contain:

• 27 Grade-A cells
• 22 Grade-B cells
• 2 Grade-C cells

These grades never modify the core priority score or rank. A high-priority cell can still carry caveats, while a lower-priority cell may have exceptionally strong supporting evidence.

Historical 2017→2025 vegetation-to-built transitions are also shown as explanatory context only. They can help a user understand how a location may have changed, but they do not increase a cell's priority.

WHAT THE USER CAN DO

The interactive web product lets a first-time visitor move through several levels of explanation.

At the pilot level, users can compare Priority, persistent daytime Heat, Greening Need, and Evidence Strength.

They can reveal whole-area 10 m land-cover evidence or reliable historical vegetation-to-built transition pixels.

Selecting an individual 500 m cell then explains whether it behaves as a heat-led candidate, greening-led candidate, mixed-signal candidate, or a strong heat-plus-greening overlap case.

The Evidence view exposes core observation count, hottest-quartile recurrence, leave-one-date-out sensitivity, stricter-QA agreement, spatial footprint support, current land-cover composition, historical support, and explicit caveats.

TECHNOLOGY

The geospatial and scientific pipeline was developed primarily in Python using Rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn. Google Earth Engine was used for satellite-data access and preprocessing.

The product uses a NestJS read-only evidence API with shared TypeScript contracts, a Next.js frontend, and MapLibre GL for interactive geographic rendering. MapTiler provides geographic basemap context.

The deployed product does not require live machine-learning inference or live Earth Engine processing. It consumes frozen, validated evidence artifacts so that the demonstrated result is reproducible and does not change during judging.

WHY WE THINK THE APPROACH IS CREATIVE

Urban heat maps and vegetation maps already exist. Our contribution is not pretending that combining those two concepts is new.

Instead, ShadeShift treats validation decisions as part of the product itself.

One NASA thermal source failed our persistence test and was downgraded. Another source survived and was promoted. A spatial bug changed our Top 10 and forced us to reopen the pipeline. Evidence grades remain separate from the planning score rather than being turned into an opaque confidence number.

Our final insight is therefore not simply “hot areas with little vegetation should receive attention.”

It is that heat and vegetation deficit are different spatial signals. Some local cells are heat-led, some are greening-led, and only some represent strong overlap. Useful prioritization depends both on that relationship and on whether the evidence behind the cell remains stable enough to trust.

INTENDED IMPACT AND LIMITATIONS

ShadeShift is designed as a first-pass investigation tool. A planner with limited resources can use it to identify which local cells deserve more detailed field assessment rather than treating every part of the pilot equally.

It does not replace local surveys, ownership information, planting feasibility, infrastructure constraints, or public-health analysis. It does not predict the number of degrees a location would cool after an intervention.

The current project is intentionally a small Thủ Đức experiment. A future expansion would test whether the same validation discipline, rather than merely the same scoring formula, remains reliable across more diverse areas of Ho Chi Minh City.
